Summary: Again and again, archaeology has caught up with the Bible. Inscriptions name Pontius Pilate and the house of David; the cities, customs, and coins of the biblical world match the text's details. Archaeology cannot prove every miracle, but it keeps confirming that the Bible is rooted in real history, not legend.
KeyPoints: The Pilate inscription confirms a Gospel figure; The Tel Dan inscription names the house of David; Biblical geography and customs check out

Summary: The most personal evidence for Christianity is transformation: addicts freed, enemies reconciled, the proud humbled, the despairing given hope. Skeptics like C. S. Lewis and Lee Strobel set out to refute the faith and were converted by it. Changed lives do not prove every doctrine, but they show the Gospel does what it promises.
KeyPoints: Conversion transforms character and conduct; Skeptics have been converted by the evidence; The Gospel's power is experiential evidence

Summary: Living cells run on information. DNA stores instructions with a four-letter code, copied, proofread, and executed by molecular machines of staggering complexity. Information of this kind always traces back to a mind in our experience, and the cell's information-rich design points to a Designer rather than unguided chance.
KeyPoints: DNA contains coded information; Codes and machines point to minds; Unguided processes have no observed power to write such code

Summary: Within years of the crucifixion, Jewish followers of Jesus were worshiping on Sunday, baptizing in His name, and sharing a meal proclaiming His death - practices that broke deeply held Jewish customs. Something enormous must explain why monotheistic Jews began worshiping a crucified man as Lord, and the resurrection is the explanation the early church itself gave.
KeyPoints: Sunday worship broke Sabbath custom; Baptism and the Lord's Supper centered on Jesus; Jews worshiping Jesus demands an explanation

Summary: Centuries before Jesus, Hebrew prophets described a Messiah born in Bethlehem, rejected by His own, pierced for others' sins, and silent before His accusers. Jesus fulfilled these specific predictions in ways no one could stage-manage. Prophecy fulfilled is God's signature across history.
KeyPoints: Micah named Bethlehem seven centuries early; Isaiah 53 describes a suffering servant; Psalm 22 pictures crucifixion before it was invented

Summary: We treat human life as possessing inherent worth - the unborn, the disabled, the dying, the enemy - in ways that go beyond usefulness. If humans are cosmic accidents, dignity is a polite fiction; if we bear God's image, dignity is real and inalienable. The Christian story grounds the worth every conscience already feels.
KeyPoints: Human worth is treated as inherent, not earned; Usefulness cannot ground dignity; The image of God grounds it
RelatedTopics: Human Dignity; Image of God; Sanctity of Life

Summary: The New Testament survives in more than 5,000 Greek manuscripts, some within decades of the originals - far more, and far earlier, than any other ancient work. Textual variants are overwhelmingly trivial, and no core doctrine hangs on a disputed reading. We can be confident the text we hold is the text they wrote.
KeyPoints: Over 5,000 Greek manuscripts survive; Some fragments date within decades of writing; Variants do not affect core doctrines

Summary: The Gospels read like reports from people who were there: named eyewitnesses, vivid local detail, Aramaic phrases, and embarrassing admissions the authors would not invent. Early creeds embedded in Paul's letters date to within a few years of the events. The Gospels are historical documents, not myths grown over centuries.
KeyPoints: Eyewitness detail and local color abound; Early creeds date to within years of the events; Embarrassing details signal honesty
RelatedPeople: Matthew; John the Apostle; Simon Peter

Summary: Across cultures and centuries, people report encountering God - in prayer, in worship, in crisis, and in quiet conviction - and emerging changed. While any single experience could be questioned, the sheer breadth and life-transforming fruit of such experiences, consistent with Scripture's picture of God, counts as real evidence, not mere emotion.
KeyPoints: God-encounters are widely reported across cultures; They often produce lasting moral transformation; Scripture presents a God who meets people

Summary: Beauty moves us in ways usefulness cannot explain. A sunset, a symphony, a mountain valley - these stir awe, longing, and gratitude that point beyond themselves. If the world were only atoms and accident, beauty's power to arrest us would be a strange surplus; in a world made by a beautiful Creator, it is a whisper of home.
KeyPoints: Beauty is universal and deeply moving; It points beyond mere survival value; A beautiful Creator explains our response to beauty

Summary: We do not merely process information; we experience it - colors, pain, joy, and the sense of being a self. Consciousness is stubbornly resistant to purely physical explanation: brain activity correlates with experience but does not obviously produce the inner life we know firsthand. A universe made by a conscious Mind makes consciousness expected rather than miraculous.
KeyPoints: Conscious experience is real and first-person; Physics describes structure, not subjective experience; A conscious Creator explains conscious creatures
RelatedTopics: Human Nature; Soul; Image of God

Summary: Every natural desire has a corresponding real object: hunger points to food, thirst to water. Human beings also carry a deeper longing - for lasting joy, perfect love, and a home we have never seen - that nothing in this world fully satisfies. C. S. Lewis argued this longing hints that we were made for another world.
KeyPoints: Natural desires correspond to real objects; Humans long for joy nothing earthly satisfies; This longing hints we were made for God

Summary: We live as if our choices are real and we are responsible for them - and we hold others responsible too. Strict materialism struggles to ground genuine choice: if every thought is fixed by physics, deliberation is an illusion. Christianity grounds freedom in persons made in God's image, capable of real agency and real responsibility.
KeyPoints: Moral responsibility assumes real choice; Determinism makes deliberation illusory; Persons made in God's image can truly choose
RelatedTopics: Free Will; Moral Responsibility; Image of God

Summary: Love is the deepest human experience, yet materialism reduces it to chemistry serving reproduction. But self-giving love - a parent's sacrifice, a friend's loyalty, a stranger's mercy - looks like something more: a reflection of a God who is love. If love is real and ultimate, then reality is personal at its root.
KeyPoints: Self-giving love transcends mere biology; Love is treated as ultimate, not useful; A God who is love explains love's depth

Summary: Physics is written in mathematics, and mathematics keeps predicting the world with uncanny precision - from antimatter to gravitational waves. As physicist Eugene Wigner marveled, the effectiveness of mathematics is 'unreasonable' if the universe is a cosmic accident. A rational Creator writing a rational world makes the fit expected.
KeyPoints: Mathematics describes nature with stunning precision; Abstract math predicts undiscovered realities; A rational Mind explains the fit

Summary: David Hume argued miracles are by definition the least probable explanation, but that assumes what it must prove - that God does not act. If God exists, miracles are possible, and history must weigh the evidence case by case. The well-attested resurrection appearances and the church's explosive birth are exactly the kind of evidence miracles would leave.
KeyPoints: If God exists, miracles are possible; Hume's argument assumes God does not act; The resurrection evidence must be weighed, not dismissed

Summary: If our minds are only the product of blind, unguided evolution, why trust them to find truth - including the truth of that theory? Reason, logic, and the reliability of thought itself fit poorly in a universe of mere matter and chance, but they fit perfectly in a universe made by a rational God whose image we bear.
KeyPoints: Trust in reason needs a foundation; Blind processes aim at survival, not truth; A rational Creator grounds rational minds

Summary: Truth is not a preference; some things are simply true whether we like them or not. But in a universe of only matter and motion, why should there be objective, mind-independent truths at all - including the truth that materialism is true? Truth itself points to a Mind in whom truth is grounded.
KeyPoints: Objective truth exists independently of opinion; Materialism struggles to ground truth; God as Truth itself explains it

Summary: Sixty-six books, written by more than forty authors over some 1,500 years, in three languages and on three continents - yet they tell one coherent story: creation, fall, redemption, and restoration, centered on Jesus. Such unity across such diversity is remarkable on its own; Christians see the hand of one divine Author behind the human ones.
KeyPoints: 66 books across 1,500 years tell one story; The story centers on Jesus from Genesis to Revelation; Unity suggests one guiding Author

Summary: The early church had no armies, no wealth, and no political power - and its leaders were hunted, imprisoned, and killed. Yet within a generation it spread across the Roman Empire, carried by people who had everything to lose. Movements built on a known lie do not grow like that; movements built on witnessed truth do.
KeyPoints: The church grew under persecution; Its founders gained nothing worldly; Explosive growth fits a true, witnessed message
RelatedEvents: Pentecost; Martyrdom of Stephen; Paul's Missionary Journeys

Summary: Everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist - space, time, matter, and energy all came into being at a finite point in the past - so the universe has a cause beyond itself. That cause must be timeless, spaceless, immaterial, and enormously powerful, which is what Christians mean by God.
KeyPoints: Whatever begins to exist has a cause; The universe began to exist; Therefore the universe has a cause; A cause outside space and time points to God
RelatedTopics: Creation; Existence of God; The Universe

Summary: No single argument carries the whole weight, and none needs to. Like strands twisted into a rope, cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, history, and experience together make a cord no single objection easily cuts. Christianity's case is cumulative: many independent lines of evidence converging on one conclusion - that the God of the Bible is real.
KeyPoints: Each argument contributes independent weight; Converging lines strengthen the conclusion; The whole case exceeds any single part

Summary: The fundamental constants of physics - gravity, the strong nuclear force, the cosmological constant - fall within an astonishingly narrow range that permits life. Had any of them differed by a fraction, no stars, chemistry, or life could exist. Such precision is far better explained by a designing mind than by blind chance.
KeyPoints: Physical constants are balanced within a razor-thin life-permitting range; Chance alone makes this precision deeply improbable; Design by a wise Creator explains the balance
RelatedTopics: Creation; Science and Faith; The Universe

Summary: Every culture protests injustice - the innocent should not suffer, the wicked should not prosper forever - as if the world owes us a moral order it does not currently deliver. That protest only makes sense if justice is real and a final reckoning awaits. Christianity names both: a Judge, and a day.
KeyPoints: The demand for justice is universal; It assumes a moral order beyond the present; Scripture promises a final judgment

Summary: Human beings everywhere recognize objective moral truths - that torturing the innocent is wrong, that justice is good - not as mere preferences but as real obligations. Such moral facts need a grounding beyond human opinion, and a good, personal God provides it. If morality is only a human invention, then 'evil' is just a feeling, not a fact.
KeyPoints: Objective moral values exist; They cannot be grounded in mere matter or opinion; A good moral lawgiver best explains them

Summary: Anselm argued that God is the greatest conceivable being - and a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists only in thought. If God's existence is even possible, then a maximally great being exists in every possible world, including this one. The argument is debated, but it shows belief in God is rationally serious, not a leap in the dark.
KeyPoints: God is defined as a maximally great being; Existence in reality is greater than existence in thought alone; If possible, such a being must exist
RelatedTopics: Existence of God; Philosophy; Faith and Reason

Summary: Life's origin remains one of science's deepest puzzles: non-living chemistry must somehow produce self-replicating, information-bearing cells. Decades of experiments have not closed the gap between chemistry and code. The Christian claim is not 'science cannot explain it, therefore God,' but that an intelligent cause is the kind of explanation the evidence points toward.
KeyPoints: Life requires information and replication together; Experiments have not produced life from non-life; Mind is a known source of information

Summary: The strongest historical case for Christianity is the resurrection. The tomb was empty, followers who had fled in fear suddenly proclaimed a risen Jesus, skeptics like James and Paul were converted, and the movement exploded in Jerusalem itself, where the claim could have been checked. No rival explanation accounts for all these facts as well as the resurrection does.
KeyPoints: The tomb was empty; Followers reported appearances of the risen Jesus; Skeptics were converted; The church began in Jerusalem
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Simon Peter; Paul

Summary: For most of modern history, science assumed an eternal universe. The Big Bang reversed that: the universe is expanding from a beginning, and theorems like Borde-Guth-Vilenkin suggest any expanding universe must have a boundary in the past. A universe with a beginning points beyond itself to a Beginner.
KeyPoints: Expansion points back to a beginning; The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem supports a past boundary; A beginning needs a cause
RelatedTopics: Creation; The Universe; Science and Faith

Summary: Not only does the universe permit life - it permits discovery. Its laws are stable, mathematical, and open to minds that can grasp them, and our planet sits in a remarkably well-placed observatory for studying them. A universe made to be understood, by creatures made to understand, fits a Creator who invites us to explore.
KeyPoints: Nature's laws are stable and mathematical; Humans can grasp them; Discoverability fits a purposeful Creator
